summary:
Spacoust is a desktop app that turns images of Earth and space into music anyone can understand, including people who cannot see them. I designed, built and tested it on my own, with help from AI tools.

Open any image and AI identifies what it shows: an Earth photo, a scientific data map, a planet, a nebula or a galaxy. Spacoust then converts its pixels into sound: brightness becomes pitch, darkness becomes silence and colour sets the musical scale. On ozone and temperature maps, it reads the colour legend, turns every pixel into a real value and checks it against scientific limits, such as the 220 Dobson unit ozone-hole threshold. Areas that cross a limit play clashing notes and are outlined in red. I tested it on NASA Earth Observatory imagery, including El Niño sea level maps and DSCOVR views of typhoons. It also plays live USGS earthquakes.

This answers the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by making Earth data something you can hear. A spoken guide in English or Arabic explains each piece, and a built-in check estimates whether an image is real. Over 2.2 billion people live with vision impairment; Spacoust opens our planet's data to them through sound.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Spacoust is a desktop app that turns images of Earth and space into music anyone can understand, including people who cannot see them. The user opens an image and presses one button:

1. AI (OpenAI vision) identifies what the image shows: an Earth photo, a scientific data map, a planet, a nebula, a galaxy or a star field.

2. The sound engine scans the image from left to right. Brightness becomes pitch, darkness becomes silence, the main colour chooses the musical scale, edges add rhythm and the red/blue balance sets the stereo position.

3. On ozone and temperature maps, Spacoust finds the colour legend on its own, converts every pixel into a real value and checks it against scientific limits: ozone below 220 Dobson units (the standard ozone-hole definition), sea surface temperature of 26.5 °C or more (warm enough to fuel hurricanes), land surface temperature of 45 °C or more, and temperature anomalies of +2 °C or more. Areas over a limit play clashing notes with a fixed alert sound and are outlined in red.

4. A spoken narrator, in English or Arabic, explains what the listener is about to hear before each piece.

Spacoust also plays live earthquakes from the U.S. Geological Survey: louder means stronger, a low note means deep, and left/right follows west/east, while each quake flashes on a world map.

BENEFITS

- Makes Earth data accessible to blind and visually impaired people.

- Lets anyone hear a problem, such as an ozone hole, without reading a colour scale.

- Checks whether an image looks real, edited or AI-generated, using evidence inside the file (camera data, AI-generator markers, Content Credentials) plus the AI's visual view.

- Free, and runs as a single Windows app.

INTENDED IMPACT

More than 2.2 billion people live with a vision impairment (WHO). Spacoust aims to open our planet's data to them and to make changes like ozone loss or ocean warming something people can feel, not just see on a chart.

TOOLS

Python, NumPy, SciPy, OpenCV, Pillow, CustomTkinter (desktop interface), OpenAI API (image analysis and text-to-speech), USGS live earthquake feed, Natural Earth map data, PyInstaller (Windows app), GitHub and GitHub Pages (code, releases and website). Built on a single laptop. SI tools: Claude (Anthropic) assisted with code, testing and writing; OpenAI powers the in-app image analysis and the narrator voice.

NASA DATA

I tested Spacoust on NASA Earth Observatory imagery: the El Niño sea surface height anomaly map (1997 vs 2026), DSCOVR EPIC views of Typhoon In-fa from the Pacific storm season, and Antarctic sea ice imagery. The El Niño map is a real data map, so Spacoust reads its colour legend and plays the warm-water anomaly as rising notes.

CREATIVITY

Most sonification projects turn colours into pleasant music. Spacoust measures: it reads real values and turns scientific limits into sound, so a problem sounds wrong on purpose. Each kind of image gets its own sound world: Mars sounds dusty, Saturn rings like bells, galaxies circle between the speakers and stars ring once each.

WHAT I CONSIDERED

I built Spacoust on my own, so I focused on what matters most:

- Accessibility first: narrator, fixed sound signals and full keyboard control.

- Scientific honesty: values read from colours are labelled approximate, and the app never predicts earthquakes or hurricanes.

- Accuracy: tested on maps with known answers (ozone hole measured 7.5% vs 7.1% true; hurricane-warm water 27% vs 24% true).

- Trust and safety: the same image always gives the same sound, and the app was scanned clean by 60+ antivirus engines.

- Comfort: notes stay within a range that is easy on the ears.
